# Iddhikathā (Ps 3.2)
**ID:** Ps 3.2
**Section:** Paṭisambhidāmagga (ps)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Iddhikathā* ("Discussion of Psychic Powers") constitutes the second treatise of the third section (*vagga*) and the twenty-second treatise overall in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* [Frauwallner 1995; Gethin 2001; SuttaCentral]. Formulated in the characteristic Abhidhamma-style catechism of the work, the chapter opens with analytical interrogations defining psychic power and its foundations: "What is psychic power? How many psychic powers are there? How many planes of psychic power, how many bases, how many steps, how many roots are there?" (*kā iddhi? kati iddhiyo? iddhiyā kati bhūmiyo, kati pādā, kati padāni, kati mūlāni?*) [Frauwallner 1995; Norman 1983].
The treatise expounds a comprehensive ten-fold typology of psychic or supernormal powers (*iddhi*), including power through determination or resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna-iddhi*) and power through transformation (*vikubbanā-iddhi*) [Bodhi 2003; Fiordalis 2008; Gethin 2001]. It provides detailed instructions on the four bases of spiritual power (*iddhipāda*), elucidating the mind's control over material phenomena—such as traveling invisibly to the Brahmā realm by compelling and directing the body through consciousness [Nyanaponika and Bodhi 2012; Gethin 2001]. Throughout this exposition, arahants renowned for particular psychic feats are listed by name without background narrative, presuming the reader's prior familiarity with early Buddhist legends [Norman 1983].
The *Iddhikathā* builds upon earlier sutta passages concerning spiritual potency, sharing formulas with the *Iddhipāda Saṁyutta* (SN 51), the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta* (DN 2), the *Mahāsakuludāyi Sutta* (MN 77), and the *Kevaṭṭa Sutta* (DN 11) [Norman 1983; SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus matches show extensive Pali-internal text reuse with the *Visuddhimagga*, which directly quotes and expands upon the *Iddhikathā*'s tenfold schema and its meditation accounts, as well as with the commentary *Saddhammappakāsinī* (*Paṭisambhidāmagga-aṭṭhakathā*) and the *Peṭakopadesa* [Bodhi 2003; Fiordalis 2008; DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also aligns segments of the text with cross-language parallels in Buddhist Sanskrit and Tibetan treatises on supernormal powers, including Harivarman's *Satyasiddhiśāstra*, the *Śrāvakabhūmi*, and the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā* [DharmaNexus].
